extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, policymakers, and researchers interested in FCC net neutrality regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the regulatory standards and principles contained in the FCC's 2010 Open Internet Order (Part 8, 47 CFR) governing broadband providers, including the stated purpose, transparency, no-blocking, and non-discrimination requirements and their exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2005 Open Internet principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States Federal Communications Commission established four principles of "open internet" in 2005: (1) Consumers deserve access to the lawful Internet content of their choice. (2) Consumers should be allowed to run applications and use services of their choice, subject to the needs of law enforcement. (3) Consumers should be able to connect their choice of legal devices that do not harm the network. (4) Consumers deserve to choose their network providers, application and service providers, and content providers of choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tenets encapsulate the ideas of net neutrality and served as the foundational policy goals that the Open Internet Order implements and elaborates. They are descriptive policy goals rather than detailed technical rules, but guide interpretation of later specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on ISP discrimination (Genachowski 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: FCC Commissioner Julius Genachowski revamped the 2005 principles by adding the idea that internet service providers may not discriminate against content in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addition emphasizes a broad non-discrimination norm that informed the Open Internet Order's later ‘‘no unreasonable discrimination’’ and ‘‘no blocking’’ rules; it functions as policy rationale for stricter treatment of ISP traffic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose (§8.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: §8.1 Purpose. The purpose of this Part is to preserve the Internet as an open platform enabling consumer choice, freedom of expression, end-user control, competition, and the freedom to innovate without permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory/policy purpose statement sets the objectives that the rules (§8.3, §8.5, §8.7) are intended to achieve and is used to interpret permissible and impermissible provider conduct under the Order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency (§8.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: §8.3 Transparency. A person engaged in the provision of broadband Internet access service shall publicly disclose accurate information regarding the network management practices, performance, and commercial terms of its broadband Internet access services sufficient for consumers to make informed choices regarding use of such services and for content, application, service, and device providers to develop, market, and maintain Internet offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure requirement is limited: the rule does not require public disclosure of competitively sensitive information or information that would compromise network security or undermine the efficacy of reasonable network management practices. The transparency rule was upheld by the D.C. Circuit when other rules were vacated.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Blocking (§8.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: §8.5 No Blocking. A person engaged in the provision of fixed broadband Internet access service... shall not block lawful content, applications, services, or non-harmful devices, subject to reasonable network management. A person engaged in the provision of mobile broadband Internet access service... shall not block consumers from accessing lawful websites, subject to reasonable network management; nor shall such person block applications that compete with the provider's voice or video telephony services, subject to reasonable network management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule distinguishes fixed and mobile broadband: fixed providers are prohibited from blocking lawful content, apps, services, or non-harmful devices; mobile providers are prohibited from blocking access to lawful websites and from blocking applications that compete with the provider's voice/video telephony services. All blocking prohibitions are qualified by the "subject to reasonable network management" exception. The D.C. Circuit later vacated the Order's no-blocking provision in Verizon v. FCC (2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: No Unreasonable Discrimination (§8.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: §8.7 No Unreasonable Discrimination. A person engaged in the provision of fixed broadband Internet access service... shall not unreasonably discriminate in transmitting lawful network traffic over a consumer's broadband Internet access service. Reasonable network management shall not constitute unreasonable discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies explicitly to fixed broadband providers. The rule forbids "unreasonable" discrimination (not all discrimination) and expressly carves out reasonable network management as permissible. Determinations of what is "unreasonable" depend on context and the claimed need for management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two classes of internet access; differential treatment for fixed vs. wireless
rubrics_metrics.description: The Open Internet Order "creates two classes of internet access, one for fixed-line providers and the other for the wireless Net." The regulations adopt an aggressive net neutrality stance towards fixed-line broadband providers but a more lenient approach towards wireless providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FCC rationale: wireless carriers are regulated far more loosely because their service is more constrained by technical limitations than fixed-line connections. This bifurcated approach affects how strictly the Transparency, No Blocking, and No Unreasonable Discrimination rules apply across service types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable network management (caveat/exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Across the rules the Order qualifies obligations with the concept of "reasonable network management": practices and exceptions are permitted when they are reasonable and necessary to manage the network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in §8.3, §8.5, and §8.7. Network management activities that are necessary for security, network integrity, congestion management, or other legitimate technical reasons may be allowed; the transparency rule exempts disclosure of information that would compromise network security or undermine the efficacy of reasonable network management. The Order treats reasonable management as not amounting to "unreasonable discrimination."
